query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Using a feedstock with a higher average particle size (i.e., shifting the particle size distribution to target larger particles) will increase deposition efficiency and enable the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat to attain the required thickness without compromising coating integrity or promoting excess as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy powder with a nominal 15–45 μm particle size distribution used for thermal-spray deposition of bond coats.
generation.intervention: Replace the existing 15–45 μm feedstock with a feedstock possessing a higher average particle size (e.g., shifting towards a 30–60 μm distribution).
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition under standard operational settings for thermal barrier coating systems and service conditions typical of high-temperature, thermally cycled applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle momentum due to increased mass, leading to more effective splat formation and reduced in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Larger particles retain higher kinetic energy upon impact, resulting in improved flattening and adherence; concurrently, their shorter residence time in the high-temperature plume minimizes oxidation, thus preserving the coating's microstructural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The deposit will exhibit a significantly increased thickness relative to coatings produced from the 15–45 μm feedstock, while maintaining minimal oxidation and robust mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock, which do not reliably reach the required thickness while preserving minimal oxidation and optimal adhesion.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain effective under conventional thermal-spray operational parameters and typical high-temperature service conditions, though extreme deviations in spray settings or environmental conditions may affect the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of the thickness improvement and its trade-off with oxidation levels requires experimental verification under controlled standard conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of coatings under identical thermal-spray conditions: one using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock and one using the feedstock with the increased average particle size (e.g., 30–60 μm). Compare the resulting coatings for thickness, oxidation levels, and mechanical integrity.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional imaging and thickness analysis)
Surface oxidation levels (using XPS or EDS analysis)
Adhesion and cohesion (evaluated by standardized mechanical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced from the larger-particle feedstock does not achieve a measurable increase in thickness (e.g., less than a 10% improvement) or if it exhibits significantly higher oxidation or compromised adhesion compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Shifting the feedstock particle size distribution to include a larger average diameter (for example, targeting 30–60 μm particles instead of the current 15–45 μm) will improve deposition efficiency to achieve the required coating thickness while still preserving the coating’s microstructural integrity and limiting as-sprayed oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy powder with a nominal particle size distribution of 15–45 μm used as thermal-spray feedstock
drafts.intervention: Replace the existing feedstock with one having a higher average particle size (i.e. a tighter distribution around 30–60 μm)
drafts.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition under standard operational settings used for applying bond coats in thermal barrier coating systems, and service conditions typical for high-temperature, thermally cycled applications
drafts.structural_mediator: Increased particle momentum and reduced in‐flight residence time mediate improved splat formation and rapid deposition, leading to thicker builds with preserved microstructure
drafts.mechanism: Larger particles possess greater mass and momentum so that upon impact they retain higher kinetic energy, which results in better flattening and adherence, thereby increasing deposition efficiency. Their reduced exposure time to the high-temperature spray plume limits oxidation, preserving coating integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The deposit will achieve a significantly increased thickness (relative to the baseline coating from 15–45 μm feedstock) without incurring additional oxidation or a compromise in adhesion and cohesion quality.
drafts.baseline: The bond coat deposited from the 15–45 μm feedstock, which fails to attain the required thickness while maintaining minimal oxidation and coating integrity.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to remain effective at typical thermal-spray process conditions and under the service conditions of high thermal cycling; extreme adjustments in spray parameters or environment may alter the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled thermal-spray experiment where two sets of coatings are produced: one using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock and one using the feedstock with the shifted distribution (e.g., 30–60 μm). All other spray environment, operational parameters, and substrate conditions should be held constant.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional optical or electron microscopy measurements)
Oxidation level (using surface oxidation analysis such as XPS or EDS)
Adhesion and cohesion strength (via standardized mechanical adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced with the larger feedstock particles does not show a significant increase in thickness (e.g., less than a 10% improvement over the baseline) or if measurements indicate increased oxidation levels or compromised adhesion compared with the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
